PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family
Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, hereby present this
84th Report of the Committee on the Demand for Grants (Demand No. 06) of the Ministry of AYUSH, for
the year 2015-16.
2. The Committee held one sitting, on 31st March, 2015 for examination of Demands for Grants -
2015-16 of the Ministry of AYUSH and heard the Secretary (AYUSH) and other Officers thereon.
3. The Committee considered the Draft Report and adopted the same in its meeting held on 23rd April,
2015.
4. The Committee while making its observations/recommendations has mainly relied upon the following
documents:
(i) Address by the President of India to both Houses of Parliament assembled together on 23rd
February, 2015;
(ii) Speech of Finance Minister on 28lh February, 2015 while presenting the Union Budget 2015-
16;
(iii) Implementation of Budget Announcements 2014-15;
(iv) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Ministry of AYUSH for the year 2015-16;
(v) Annual Report of the Ministry for the year 2014-15;
(vi) Outcome Budget of the Ministry for the year 2015-16;
(vii) Detailed Explanatory Note on Demands for Grants of the Ministry of AYUSH for the year
2015-16;
(viii) Physical and financial targets fixed and achievements made so far during the Twelfth Plan
period;
(ix) Projection of outlays for the schemes to be undertaken by the Ministry during the remaining
years of the Twelfth Five Year Plan;
(x) Details of under-utilization of the allocations made under different heads during the last three
years;
(xi) Written replies furnished by the Ministry to the Questionnaires sent to them by the Secretariat;
(xii) Presentation made by the Secretary (AYUSH) and other concerned officers; and
(xiii) W ritten clarifications furnished by the Ministry, on the points/issues raised by the Members
during the deliberations of the Committee.
5. For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the Committee have
been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

REPORT
Introduction
1. The Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (ISM&H) was established as a
separate Department under Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India in 1995. It was
renamed as Department of Ayurveda, Yoga & Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy (AYUSH) in
November, 2003. The Department of AYUSH has now been made an independent Ministry w.e.f. 09.11.2014.
The Ministry is mandated for policy, planning and program implementation for growth, development and
propagation of AYUSH systems across national and international fronts. Sowa Rigpa is the recent inclusion
to the family of AYUSH systems. The Ministry under its purview has National Institutes, Research Councils,
Regulatory Bodies, Pharmacopoieal Laboratories, Pharmacopoeia Commission, medicines manufacturing
enterprise and National Medicinal Plants Board.
2. The Twelfth Five Year Plan aims at promoting the health goals with appropriate utilization of AYUSH
in the health delivery system based on their strength areas and interventions for health promotion and
management of disease burden.
3. All the existing Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS) have been merged into a single umbrella Scheme
namely, National AYUSH Mission (NAM) and introduced w.e.f. 29.09.2014.
4. The scope of Pharmacopoeia Commission of Indian Medicine was expanded to include Homoeopathy
in its purview with necessary fundamental changes in the structure for smooth performance.
5. Approval of National AYUSH Mission, as a unified Centrally Sponsored Scheme, will help to support
implementation of state programs and projects with more flexibility and better funding pattern. Revised
Central Schemes for public health interventions of AYUSH, Extra Mural Research, Development of Industry
Clusters, promotional activities of AYUSH, International co-operation and incentive to the industry are meant
for propelling propagation of AYUSH in tandem with the public aspirations and needs.
6. The proposed budget amounting to Rs.1008 crore for the financial year 2015-16 would be utilized for
comprehensive development of AYUSH sector. Further, the outcomes would go a long way in giving much
needed boost towards providing health care services and global leadership of the country in the field of
traditional medicine.
7. The Ministry under its purview has two Regulatory Councils, five Research Councils, seven National
Institutes, two Pharmacopeia Laboratories, a National Medicinal Plants Board and a public sector undertaking
for manufacture of Ayurveda & Unani medicine.
8. During the Twelfth Plan period, the Ministry seeks to strengthen initiatives taken earlier to expand the
reach of health care through Traditional Systems of Medicine. The Twelfth Plan duly recognized the fact
that the strengths of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, if suitably used, can help advance the
goals of the Twelfth Plan. AYUSH systems would be main-streamed using their areas of strengths namely in
preventive and promotive health care, diseases and health conditions relating to women and children, older
persons, Non-communicable diseases, preventive health care, mental ailments, stress management, palliative
care, rehabilitation and health promotion.

10. A perusal of the budget allocation made for the six years from April, 2007 to March, 2013, the
Committee notes that total allocation of Rs. 4849 crores was made for the Department of AYUSH and out of
this amount only 76% i.e. Rs. 3709 crores could be spent. The Committee fails to comprehend this state of
consistent under-utilization when a lot of work is still required to be accomplished by AYUSH, namely
efficacy and quality of AYUSH drugs are still to be brought under Controller, education for producing
AYUSH Doctors and allied staff is in a bad shape and the Department has failed in bringing a legislation for
creating a regulatory authority for control and regulation of AYUSH system of Health care, quality of drugs
and education/training for producing adequate manpower.

14. As is evident from the table above, a Plan Outlay of Rs. 10044.00 Crore was made for the entire
Twelfth Plan Period. For the first three years of the Plan Period i.e. from 2012-13 to 2014-15, an amount of
Rs. 3128 crores was allocated on plan side which was reduced to Rs. 1820.26 crore at RE stage and the
actual expenditure during these three years (as on 28-2-2015) was Rs. 1470.25 crores. The Committee
notes that owning to drastic reduction of allocations at RE stage in the first three years of 12th Plan and even
lesser actual expenditure, the Ministry was able to utilize only 15% of the total Twelfth Plan approved outlay.
The Committee fails to understand as to how with this trend of utilization the Ministry will do justice with
the total allocations.
15. The Ministry has adduced the following reasons for underutilization of budgeted funds under various
schemes:
(i) Non-filling of posts;
(ii) Schemes are yet to be approved;
(iii) Reduction in allocation at RE stage
(iv) unspent balance;

6
(v) Pending Utilization Certificates;
(vi) Delay in execution of evaluation work;
(vii) Non-receipt of adequate and eligible proposals
(viii) Slow pace of construction; etc.
16. Explaining the persistent under-utilization of allocated funds over the years, the Secretary (AYUSH)
during his evidence before the Committee on 31st March, 2015, attributed the main reasons for less utilization
of funds to structural weaknesses of State AYUSH Institutions, less absorption capacity of the States and
pending Utilization Certificates.
17. The Secretary also enumerated the following steps taken to ensure that the un-utilized balance is
minimized.
(i) The Ministry has comprehensively reviewed the expenditure profile of each major scheme/
programme before preparing the budget estimates.
(ii) Timely release and assimilation of funds by State Governments/ Institutes/Councils and other
organizations, is being emphasized.
(iii) Nodal Officers for individual States have been nominated by Ministry of AYUSH to follow-up
the matter with individual States for liquidation of outstanding UCs.
(iv) Regular meetings with state officials are held at the level of Secretary (AYUSH) to emphasize
and ensure optimal and efficient utilization of funds. In the first-ever meeting of state AYUSH
Ministers Chaired by Hon'ble Minister (IC), AYUSH the issue of pending Utilization Certificates
has also been reviewed.
(v) Scheme-wise Roadmaps for future utilisation of funds have been drawn for efficient and
timely utilization of funds - particularly in the first and second quarter of the next financial year
and identify possible bottlenecks well in advance and address the same. For example, emphasis
is laid on holding of the regular meetings of Mission Directorate, Project Screening Committee
(PSC), Technical Screening Committee (TSC) and Standing Finance Committee (SFC) etc.
for various schemes, well in advance so as to ensure timely release of funds in 2015-16.
(vi) One of the flagship schemes, the National AYUSH Mission (NAM), was approved and notified
on 29.09.2014. NAM focuses on implementation efficiency and improving absorption capacity
of the States through setting up of State AYUSH Societies and strengthening of State Programme
Management Units with adequate staff and infrastructure for implementing and monitoring the
mission activities. One of the criteria for deciding the allocation 'envelop' to the states is their
track record in utilizing funds in the past.
(vii) Action plan from 27 States for Rs. 185.72 already sanctioned. The required budget Head for
NAM has already been created. Out of Rs. 185.72 crore merely Rs. 9.90 crore could be
released so far. Around Rs.120 crore is estimated to be released for already approved NAM
action plans in the first quarter of the next year itself against a total annual allocation of Rs.318
crore.
(viii) The Ministry is also working to support the States to strengthen the institutional framework
and improve capacity for better leverage and efficacy in utilization of funds. For example,

7
under NAM, there is a specific component for strengthening State Programme Management
Units. The 21 States/ UTs have already intimated the constitutions of State AYUSH Societies
and other states/ UTs are also gearing up for the constitution of AYUSH Societies. Similarly
support to State Medicinal Plant Boards has been significantly increased under the revised
Central Sector Scheme Guidelines of the NMPB.
18. The Secretary also drew attention of the Committee to the changeover from the Society route of
funds to the Treasury Route in the financial year 2014-15. He stated that earlier the funds were released to
the State Health Societies directly. As per the new arrangement, funds have to go to the State Budgets. The
State Governments have to contribute their share and draw that amount and pass it on to the Health societies.
The Secretary submitted that in the direct transmission of money from the Central Government to the State
Health Society through the Treasury Route, UC conditionality is not an absolute bar for release of funds. He
also submitted that the problems have now been largely ironed out and utilization rate of funds is expected
to increase in the financial year 2015-16 because all the Centrally Sponsored Schemes are to be funded
through the Treasury Route. Highlighting the weak AYUSH structures in the States, the Secretary informed
the Committee that in the entire country only two States, namely Uttarakhand and Rajasthan have separate
AYUSH Departments. 25 of 36 States/UTs have AYUSH Directorates which are not at par with the full-
fledged Department.

22. The Committee is concerned to find that there were savings of significant magnitude under
several important heads during 2013-14 and 2014-15 as is evident from Table Nos. 2 and 3 given
above. The fact that the savings were not just the result of implementation of economy measures
but occurred due to various reasons like non-filing of posts, non-approval of schemes, delay in
execution work, slow space of construction etc, clearly suggests that there were inadequacies in the
monitoring mechanism, as well as budgetary planning process and budget allocations were proposed
without obtaining all necessary clearances. The Committee is of the firm view that the savings
would have been minimized substantially if proper internal auditing and streamlined monitoring
mechanisms had been in place and periodic review of the trends and progress of expenditure had
been adopted. The Committee notes that the Ministry of AYUSH has initiated, at the behest of this
Committee, a number of steps to ensure optimal and efficient utilization of allotted funds. The
Committee would like the Ministry to scrupulously implement the initiatives taken in this regard
and simultaneously evaluate the impact of new initiatives on utilization of budgeted funds. The
Committee would like to be kept apprised of the impact of the new initiatives taken on utilization
of budgeted funds.
23. The Committee is constrained to note that there has been persistent and substantial
underutilization of Plan funds under the heads - "Hospitals and Dispensaries", "Educational
Institutions", "Research and Development including Medicinal Plants", "Development of AYUSH
Industry", and "National Mission on AYUSH". The allocations made in BE 2013-14 and BE 2014-15
under the above heads, were subsequently revised downwards at the RE stage and the sums which
remained grossly underutilized, were surrendered by the end of the year. The Committee observes
that such huge variations in BE, RE and Actuals are indicative of the fact that principles of fiscal
prudence and discipline were neither observed nor proper assessment of the projects was carried
out. The Committee observes that in a resource-constrained country like India, all care needs to be
taken to ensure that the scarce resources do not remain locked up and surrendered at the fiscal
end. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry chalk out its fiscal roadmap in such
a way that the allocated funds are utilized optimally and more productively under the above Heads
and such a situation does not recur in future.
24. From a scrutiny of information furnished, it is revealed that the entire budgeted plan funds
had to be surrendered due to non-approval of certain Schemes. For example, a sum of Rs. 4.00 crore
and Rs. 25.00 crore had been proposed in BE 2013-14 and BE 2014-15 respectively under the head
"All India Institute of Unani Medicine." The Ministry spent a meagre Rs. 0.20 crore in 2013-14
while the entire budgeted funds for 2014-15 had to be surrendered due to non-approval of the
project. What is alarming is that this is not the only example of surrender of the entire budgeted
funds. Similar is the case with quite a few other projects such as "All India Institute of Yoga", "All
India Institute of Homoeopathy", "Homoeopathic Medicines Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd",
"Pharmacovigilance Initiative for ASU drugs", "National Institute of Medicinal Plants", etc. The
Committee deprecates the Ministry for making unrealistic projection of fund requirements without
obtaining necessary approvals for implementation of the above projects. The Committee, therefore,
strongly recommends that the Ministry should ensure that all pre-approval formalities are completed
before budget allocations are proposed and realistic financial outlays are earmarked for the above
projects/schemes. There is no point in making ritualistic allocations which remain on paper only.
25. The Committee observes that to obtain greater evenness in the budgeted expenditure within
a financial year and reduce rush of expenditure in the last quarter of the financial year, Ministry of

9
Finance has prescribed the expenditure ceiling of 33% for the last quarter of the financial year. As
is evident from Table No. 5, the Ministry of AYUSH has breached the ceiling of 33%, though only
marginally, by incurring expenditure of 36.61% of plan funds in the last quarter. The Committee
would like the Ministry to monitor expenditure of funds more closely and avoid rush of expenditure
in the last quarter.
26. The Committee notes with concern that out of the plan allocation of Rs. 1069.00 crore each in
BE 2013-14, and BE 2014-15, as much as Rs. 507.99 Crore and Rs. 573.21 Crore were surrendered in

Updation of Central Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy
47. The updation of Central Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy has been engaging the attention
of the Committee for quite some time. In reply to a question regarding the status of updation of Central
Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy, the Ministry has furnished the following information
(Annexure - 1). On being asked about the time lag between the receipt of information from the State
Governments and its updation into the Central Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoeopathy, the Ministry
have furnished the following information:
"As regards time lag of updation in the Central Registers of Indian Medicine, it is informed that the procedure
for entry of information received from the State Boards/Councils to Central Register takes at least four to six
months depending on the number of practitioners registered in the State Register because the procedure
includes, inter alia, that:
(i) State Register is screened keeping in view that all the particulars fulfilling the requirement of
the CCIM of the registered practitioners are furnished in respective columns;
(ii) Further screening of the State Register is done to ensure that the practitioners are possessing
recognized medical qualification of Ayurveda, Unani and Siddha included in the Schedules to
IMCC Act, 1970;
(iii) Translation of Central Register of Indian Medicine from English to Hindi or vice versa;
(iv) Thereafter the Central Register is typed bilingually in English and Hindi and compared to the
State Register in order to ensure the correctness of the same; and
(v) The prepared Central Register in English and Hindi is sent/submitted to the Controller of
Publication, Deptt. of Publication, Govt, of India for its Gazette Notification in the Gazette of
India.
48. Regarding time lag of updation in the Central Registers of Homoeopathy, it is informed that the state
Registers, as and when received, are scrutinized and'as required, clarifications are sought by C.C.H. from
State Boards/ Councils which require some time. However, on an average taking data from State Register to
Central Register consumes three months to 24 months in view of the said reason."
49. The Committee regrets to note that despite its earlier recommendation to timely update the
Central Registers of the Indian systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, not much headway has
been made in the matter, mainly due to delay in submission of accurate information by the State
Boards and its incorporation in the Central Registers. This is contrary to a provision in the Indian
Medicine Central Council (IMCC) Act 1970 which mandates the State Boards to submit updated
registers of practitioners on the first of April every year. The Committee is also dismayed to note
from the information furnished that the data received from the States is often found to have several
inaccuracies which further delays the updation of the Registers. The Committee is also surprised to
note that the time-lag between the receipt of information from the State Governments and its
updation /incorporation is 6 to 9 months in respect of the Central Register of Indian Medicine and
3 to 24 months in respect of the Central Register of Homoeopathy. Given the IT resources currently
available, the Committee is unable to reconcile itself with this huge time-lag. The Committee
would, therefore, recommend that the Ministry should initiate action, both statutory and
administrative, to facilitate timely maintenance and submission of accurate information and its
incorporation in both the Central Registers of the Indian systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy.
The Committee would like to be apprised of the action initiated in this regard.

Issues concerning regulation of Naturopathy and Yoga
63. On being asked whether there is any mechanism in place for registration of Practitioners of Naturopathy
and Yoga, the Committee has been informed that presently there was no provision for registration of
Naturopathy & Yoga practitioners at Central Government level. However, some of the State Governments
like Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamilnadu, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and West Bengal
have provision for registration of such practitioners for BNYS graduates. The Central Government had
issued guidelines in the year 2006. In 2014 again, the Ministry had circulated a concept note on this subject
to all the State Governments, Universities & Colleges, and other stake holders. Based on the feedback
received in response thereto, the shape and structure of future mechanism for registration is under deliberation.
The then Department of AYUSH had decided in 2006, not to regulate Yoga and Naturopathy at Central level
on the basis of the following considerations:
(a) The CCIM did not agree to the proposed inclusion of Yoga and Naturopathy in their mandate
on the plea that it had nothing common with other systems namely Ayurveda, Siddha and
Unani.
(b) Setting up of separate Central Council for Yoga and Naturopathy was not agreed to on the
grounds that there were only few practitioners in the field of Yoga and Naturopathy and limited
infrastructure, which does not justify a separate Regulatory Body.
64. The Ministry also informed the Committee that the issue of regulation of Yoga & Naturopathy is
under deliberation.
65. The Committee observes that Naturopathy and Yoga are gaining popularity not only amongst
the Indians but all over the world and feels that there is an urgent need to regulate the practice of
Naturopathy and Yoga. Some guidelines/norms should be prescribed in this regard and the people
should be made aware of the benefit of these practices but under the guidance of the trained
manpower.

National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB)
92. The increasing global interest in natural remedies has increased the demand for medicinal plants. The
resource base for AYUSH is largely plants which are largely sourced from the wild areas. This has led to the
emergence of a number of issues like sustainability, conservation, cultivation, quality assurance, protection
of Traditional Knowledge and related issues of access and benefit sharing etc. To coordinate all these
matters, Government of India established the National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB) under the Department
of AYUSH in 2000. NMPB is the apex national body which co-ordinates all matters relating to medicinal
plants in the country and provides financial support to programmes relating to conservation, cultivation and
the all-round development of the medicinal plants sector.

Quality Control of ASU&H Drugs
101. As per information furnished to the Committee, the Ministry of AYUSH has a Drug Regulatory Cell.
The Cell is responsible for handling regulatory and quality control matters of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and
Homoeopathy (ASU and H) drugs. The AYUSH system of Medicine is governed by the Drugs and Cosmetics
Act 1940 and the Rules thereunder. Enforcement of the provisions contained under Chapter IV A of the Act
is the responsibility of the State Governments. In superintending the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics
Act, 1940 and Rules thereunder and Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act 1954 in
relation to ASU and H drugs, the Drug Control Cell coordinates with the State Licensing Authorities and
Drug Controllers to achieve uniform administration of the legal provisions and for providing regulatory
guidance and clarification to the States. It also undertakes program management and examination of State
Annual Plans for Quality Control under National AYUSH Mission (NAM) through which grant-in-aid is
provided for improving infrastructure and functional capacity of Drug Testing Laboratories, Pharmacies
and Enforcement Mechanism in the States.
102. During the course of examination of Demands for Grants (2013-14) the Ministry of AYUSH (erstwhile
Department of AYUSH) had admitted that due to weak organizational set-ups in the State AYUSH Directorates
and Licensing Authorities, the utilization of grants released under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for
Quality Control has not been up to the mark. The problem of non-submission of Utilization Certificates
deprived the States of availing any more financial assistance for improving the quality control measures. The
compliance to Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) by ASU and H drug manufacturers and its enforcement
by the State regulators is not in the desired perspective. Besides, drug testing facilities in the States are
inadequate to meet the regulatory needs because of the infrastructural bottlenecks in the State Drugs Testing
Laboratories and scarcity of Approved Drug Testing Laboratories and Capacities.
103. On being asked about the allocation for quality control of AYUSH drugs for 2015-16, the Secretary
during his evidence replied that out of Rs. 318.00 Crore allocated for the Centrally Sponsored Schemes
about sixteen crores of rupees will be available for the quality control of AYUSH drugs for all the States
together, which will work out to Rs. 20.00 to Rs. 30.00 Lakhs for each State.
104. In reply to a question the Ministry has informed that 19 proposals from 19 States have been received
out of which proposals from 12 States, viz. Orissa, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh,
Rajasthan, Tripura, West Bengal, Haryana and Arunachal Pradesh, Assam and Andaman Nicobar Islands
have been approved and the proposal of remaining 7 States, viz. Punjab, Maharashtra, Meghalaya, Jharkhand,
Karnataka, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir are yet to be approved by NAM.
105. The Committee in its 55th Report on Demands for Grants (2012-13) of erstwhile Department
of AYUSH had inter alia observed that "the quality and standardization of ASU&H products and
stringent implementation of the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and the rules
framed thereunder are very vital for the credibility o ASU and H drugs. However, the drug testing
requirements of ASU and H drugs cannot be me without setting up adequate number of quality
control laboratories and strengthenin of the enforcement mechanisms of the States." From
information made available b the Committee, it is revealed that the Centrally Sponsored Scheme
for supportin quality control activities has been evaluated by an external agency and revised suitabi
on the basis of suggestions from the States. The Committee sincerely hopes that th revised scheme
would maximize outcome oriented implementation and lead to bette off-take under this scheme
during the remaining period of the 12th Five Year Plan. Th Committee recommends that the Ministry
should closely monitor utilization of th funds under this head particularly, as it relates to capacity
building of the State Dru Testing Laboratories for better quality control of ASU and H drugs.

26
The Committee also notes that Indian Ayurvedic drugs were found containing excessive mercury
and other substance and therefore were banned by Eurpoean Union and some other Countries and
these Countries had imposed ban on Ayurvedic drugs and cosmetics which apart from bringing a bad
name to the country also resulted i loss of precious foreign exchange. The Committee recommends
that such incidents need to be avoided.
106. On being asked about the updated status of setting up a Central Regulatory Authority for ASU and H
Drugs and creating the Central Drug Controller for Ayurveda; Siddha, Unani and Homoeopathy drugs, the
Ministry in a written reply has stated th following:-
"Note for seeking approval of the Cabinet to set up a separate Central Drugs Controller of
AYUSH was sent to the Cabinet Secretariat on 9th October, 2014. The note has been received
back on 11.2.2015 with the advice from PMO for Minister of Health and Family Welfare to
hold a meeting with Secretary (AYUSH), Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and
Drug Controller General of India to consider and recommend whether a full-fledged Drug
Controller General for AYUSH is required or whether there is possibility of a wing for AYUSH,
manned by experts from AYUSH field placed under the existing Drug Controller General of
India. Meeting was held on 05.03.2015 wherein it was decided to develop a vertical structure
of AYUSH in the present Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) headed by
Drugs Controller General (India)".
107. During the course of examination of Demands for Grants (2013-14), the Ministry of AYUSH, on
being asked as to why it is not desirable to let CDSCO regulate ASU Drugs, had submitted that CDSCO has
been basically dealing with quality control of allopathic drugs and accordingly, the whole paraphernalia there
does not have the wherewithal to effectively regulate ASU&H drugs. The basic reason is that ASU&H drugs
are distinct from allopathic drugs in terms of philosophy, principles, concepts, standards, quality aspects,
applications, numbers and count of manufacturing units and testing requirements, hence they need to have
different regulations. Inspite of common Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, the regulatory issues of ASU&H
drugs are not being taken care of by the Central Drugs Controller Office due to non-availability of requisite
expertise and huge workload of matters related to allopathic drugs. The idea of having a common Central
Drugs Authority with Additional Drug Controller of AYUSH had not been earlier agreed to. However, the
office of the Drug Controller General (India) was strengthened by sanctioning 175 posts for modern medicine
and was renamed as Central Drugs Standards Control Organisation (CDSCO), but no posts were sanctioned
for the Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy. It was thereafter only that in accordance with the
recommendations of a high powered Committee and ASU Drugs Consultative Committee and considering
the specific regulatory requirements of ASU&H drugs, setting up a separate Central Drugs Controller of
AYUSH was found to be a necessary requirement.
108. The Committee observes that quality control and standardization of ASU&H drugs leaves
much to be desired. It has often been reported in the media that Ayurveda and Homoeopathy drugs,
which were given to patients for various ailments, were laced with steroids and other improper
drugs. Permissible limits of heavy metals, pesticide residue, microbial load etc. are also sometimes
breached and regulatory needs of standardization and quality control of ASU&H drugs get seriously
impaired. On the issue of setting up of a separate Drug Controller of AYUSH, the decision to
develop a vertical structure of AYUSH in the present Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation
(CDSCO) headed by the Drug Controller General of India is not acceptable to the Committee. The
Committee feels that in order to strengthen regulatory mechanism and effectively oversee the
quality control of ASU&H drugs, setting up of a separate Central Drug Controller for ASU&H drugs

27
is an imminent necessity since a wing of AYUSH in the existing CDSCO may not produce the
desired result of effective regulation of ASU&H drugs. The Committee is of the view that a separate
Central Drugs Controller of AYUSH will help synergise the core competencies of the Central and
State Regulatory Authorities by developing dynamic relation between them and also go a long way
in building credibility in ASU&H drugs besides promoting AYUSH in foreign countries. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that action be initiated to set up an independent and separate Central Drug
Controller for ASU&H drugs at the earliest.

AYUSH drugs is vested in State Licensing Authorities and during the last six months about 125 complaints

matter. Needless to emphasise that the Ministry should continue to focus its energies on the developed
European countries and the USA for entering into MOUs so that the therapeutic credentials of
AYUSH systems of Medicine can be established globally.

strengths of AYUSH systems by using outdoor, electronic media including organization of Arogya fairs and

OBSERV ATIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS - AT A GLANCE
Budgetary Allocation
The Committee is concerned to find that there were savings of significant magnitude under
several important heads during 2013-14 and 2014-15 as is evident from Table Nos. 2 and 3 given
above. The fact that the savings were not just the result of implementation of economy measures
but occurred due to various reasons like non-filing of posts, non-approval of schemes, delay in
execution work, slow space of construction etc, clearly suggests that there were inadequacies in the
monitoring mechanism, as well as budgetary planning process and budget allocations were proposed
without obtaining all necessary clearances. The Committee is of the firm view that the savings
would have been minimized substantially if proper internal auditing and streamlined monitoring
mechanisms had been in place and periodic review of the trends and progress of expenditure had
been adopted. The Committee notes that the Ministry of AYUSH has initiated, at the behest of this
Committee, a number of steps to ensure optimal and efficient utilization of allotted funds. The
Committee would like the Ministry to scrupulously implement the initiatives taken in this regard
and simultaneously evaluate the impact of new initiatives on utilization of budgeted funds. The
Committee would like to be kept apprised of the impact of the new initiatives taken on utilization
of budgeted funds. (para 22)
The Committee is constrained to note that there has been persistent and substantial
underutilization of Plan funds under the heads - "Hospitals and Dispensaries", "Educational
Institutions", "Research and Development including Medicinal Plants", "Development of AYUSH
Industry", and "National Mission on AYUSH". The allocations made in BE 2013-14 and BE 2014-15
under the above heads, were subsequently revised downwards at the RE stage and the sums which
remained grossly underutilized, were surrendered by the end of the year. The Committee observes
that such huge variations in BE, RE and Actuals are indicative of the fact that principles of fiscal
prudence and discipline were neither observed nor proper assessment of the projects was carried
out. The Committee observes that in a resource-constrained country like India, all care needs to be
taken to ensure that the scarce resources do not remain locked up and surrendered at the fiscal
end. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry chalk out its fiscal roadmap in such
a way that the allocated funds are utilized optimally and more productively under the above Heads
and such a situation does not recur in future. (para 23)
From a scrutiny of information furnished, it is revealed that the entire budgeted plan funds
had to be surrendered due to non-approval of certain Schemes. For example, a sum of Rs. 4.00 crore
and Rs. 25.00 crore had been proposed in BE 2013-14 and BE 2014-15 respectively under the head
"All India Institute of Unani Medicine." The Ministry spent a meagre Rs. 0.20 crore in 2013-14
while the entire budgeted funds for 2014-15 had to be surrendered due to non-approval of the
project. What is alarming is that this is not the only example of surrender of the entire budgeted
funds. Similar is the case with quite a few other projects such as "All India Institute of Yoga", "All
India Institute of Homoeopathy", "Homoeopathic Medicines Pharmaceutical Co. Ltd",
"Pharmacovigilance Initiative for ASU drugs", "National Institute of Medicinal Plants", etc. The
Committee deprecates the Ministry for making unrealistic projection of fund requirements without
obtaining necessary approvals for implementation of the above projects. The Committee, therefore,

33
strongly recommends that the Ministry should ensure that all pre-approval formalities are completed
before budget allocations are proposed and realistic financial outlays are earmarked for the above
projects/schemes. There is no point in making ritualistic allocations which remain on paper only.
(para 24)
The Committee observes that to obtain greater evenness in the budgeted expenditure within
a financial year and reduce rush of expenditure in the last quarter of the financial year, Ministry of
Finance has prescribed the expenditure ceiling of 33% for the last quarter of the financial year. As
is evident from Table No. 5, the Ministry of AYUSH has breached the ceiling of 33%, though only
marginally, by incurring expenditure of 36.61% of plan funds in the last quarter. The Committee
would like the Ministry to monitor expenditure of funds more closely and avoid rush of expenditure
in the last quarter. (para 25)
The Committee notes with concern that out of the plan allocation of Rs. 1069.00 crore each in
BE 2013-14, and BE 2014-15, as much as Rs. 507.99 Crore and Rs. 573.21 Crore were surrendered in
Financial Y ears 2013-14 and 2014-15 respectively. The Committee takes a serious view of the fact
that the Ministry kept unspent budgetary provisions of Rs. 507.99 Crore in 2013-14 and Rs. 573.24
Crore in 2014-15 till the last day of the financial years despite reduction in allocations at RE stage.
The Committee observes that the unspent budgetary provisions should have been surrendered as
soon as these were foreseen without waiting till the end of the Financial Year so that they could
have been gainfully utilized under some other heads. The Committee would like the Ministry to
improve financial discipline. (para 26)
Pending Utilization Certificates
The Committee is concerned to note that the number of pending UCs and the amount involved
therein is still substantial despite the efforts made by the Ministry. What is more alarming is that
pending UCs date as far back as 2001-02. All this leads the Committee to the conclusion that the
steps taken so far have not yielded the desired results. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Ministry should review the methodology of monitoring the progress of utilization of funds
by the implementing agencies and evolve a multipronged strategy for liquidation of pending UCs so
that the execution of projects is not hamstrung by lack of flow of funds. (para 32)
The Committee takes note of the Secretary's submission that it had been decided to transfer
Central funds for Centrally Sponsored Schemes through Treasury Route instead of Society Route
and conditionally regarding submission of UCs is no longer an absolute bar for release of funds. The
Committee hopes that the new arrangement would lead to better absorption of Central funds. The
Committee, however, recommends that the Ministry should be more vigilant and ensure that the
Treasury Route of funds does not lead to fiscal profligacy and the funds so released result in
corresponding benefits and asset creation on the ground. (para 35)
Centrally Sponsored Schemes:
The Committee observes that now that the National AYUSH Mission has been approved and
implemented, the Ministry should work out modalities in consultation with all the stakeholders
including the North Eastern States to ensure that utilization of the budgeted funds for NE States
does not suffer from any inadequacies and registers a marked improvement in 2015-16. (para 44)

34
The Committee takes note of the generation of 4.8 lakhs of man-days and production of 1236
tones of Medicinal Plants in NE States under the Central Sector Schemes and welcomes the same.
The Committee would, however, expect the Ministry to monitor utilization of funds allocated for
North Eastern States in such a manner that it results in corresponding outcome. For this purpose,
the Committee would like the Ministry to put in place an on-line monitoring mechanism .
(para 45)
The Committee has learnt that there is proposal to do away with the distinction between
Special Category and Non-special Category States and if this is implemented, the 11 Special Category
States, who depend heavily on the Central Sector funds for Plan Schemes, will be hit hard as they
will end up spending much more than 10 percent and face huge shortfall in their expenditure for
health. The Committee would like to be updated in this regard. (para 46)
Updation of Central Registers of Indian Medicine and Homoepathy
The Committee regrets to note that despite its earlier recommendation to timely update the
Central Registers of the Indian systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy, not much headway has
been made in the matter, mainly due to delay in submission of accurate information by the State
Boards and its incorporation in the Central Registers. This is contrary to a provision in the Indian
Medicine Central Council (IMCC) Act 1970 which mandates the State Boards to submit updated
registers of practitioners on the first of April every year. The Committee is also dismayed to note
from the information furnished that the data received from the States is often found to have several
inaccuracies which further delays the updation of the Registers. The Committee is also surprised to
note that the time-lag between the receipt of information from the State Governments and its
updation /incorporation is 6 to 9 months in respect of the Central Register of Indian Medicine and
3 to 24 months in respect of the Central Register of Homoeopathy. Given the IT resources currently
available, the Committee is unable to reconcile itself with this huge time-lag. The Committee
would, therefore, recommend that the Ministry should initiate action, both statutory and
administrative, to facilitate timely maintenance and submission of accurate information and its
incorporation in both the Central Registers of the Indian systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy.
The Committee would like to be apprised of the action initiated in this regard. (para 49)
National Institutes under Ministry of AYUSH
National Institute of Ayurveda (NIA), Jaipur
The Committee notes with serious concern the high number of vacancies in Group 'A' posts.
Since the National Institute of Ayurveda is inter-alia mandated to develop high standards of teaching,
training and research in all aspects of Ayurvedic System of Medicine, such a large number of vacancies
in Group 'A' posts will certainly lead to compromise its mandated activities and affect the quality of
teaching and research in an adverse manner. The Committee in its 68th Report on Demands for
Grants (2013-14) had taken cognizance of the high number of vacancies and recommended filling
up of the vacancies in faculty posts with priority and urgency and also suggested action towards
appointing professionally qualified persons on short-term contract or deputation till regular
appointments are made. The Committee would further recommend that keeping in view the perennial
shortage of manpower in senior faculty positions, the Ministry may explore the possibility of
appropriately revising the methods and conditions of recruitment of senior faculty without
compromising the requisite standards. Better service conditions and emoluments may also be
considered for attracting the available talent towards teaching profession. (para 52)

35
National Institute of Homoeopathy, Kolkata
The Committee is dismayed to note that construction of Hospital Building for the purpose of
expansion of the Hospital from 100 beds to 250 beds is yet to be completed, though the original
targeted year of completion of the project was 2010-11. During the course of examination of Demands
for Grants (2013-14) in April, 2013, the Ministry had informed the Committee that the original cost

there would be no more delays and the expansion of the NIH would be executed within the revised

and the quantum of emoluments so that it would attract talent towards this profession and facilitate
filling up of vacancies. (para 57)
Morarji Desai National Institute of Yoga (MDNIY)
The Committee observes that despite incurring very little expenditure against the budgeted
plan allocations of Rs. 9.00 crore in BE 2014-15, Rs. 5.00 crore has been allocated on the plan side in
BE 2015-16. Keeping in view the fact that the shortfall in utilization of budgeted plan allocation to
the extent of Rs. 10.42 crore was also witnessed in the fiscal year 2013-14, the Committee recommends

assessing the fund requirements and its correlation with the fund deployment and utilization.

and also of the outcome thereof. (para 62)

The Committee observes that Naturopathy and Yoga are gaining popularity not only amongst
the Indians but all over the world and feels that there is an urgent need to regulate the practice of
Naturopathy and Yoga. Some guidelines/norms should be prescribed in this regard and the people
should be made aware of the benefit of these practices but under the guidance of the trained
manpower. (para 65)
North Eastern Institute of Ayurveda and Homoeopathy (NEIAH), Shillong
The Committee observes that it is a matter of serious concern that NEIAH is yet to be fully

and surrendering of the budgeted funds year after year is not only indicative of serious shortcomings

36
in the planning and monitoring mechanism of the Ministry but also reflects absence of sound
budgetary mechanism for assessing the actual requirement of funds for the on-going civil works.
The Committee also expresses its serious concern at the tardy progress made towards enabling full

the Institute and gainfully utilize the allocated funds for the purpose. (para 69)
North Eastern Institute of Folk Medicine (NEIFM), Passighat, Arunachal Pradesh
It is extremely disquieting that despite the fact that the time-line for completion of this
important project had to be revised four times, NEIFM is still not fully operationalised. The
Committee deprecates the Ministry for the inordinate delay in full operationalization of the Institute
which aims to revitalize, promote and harness local health traditions of the North Eastern Region of
the country. While expressing serious concern over the snail's pace of the progress made in the
matter, the Committee recommends that a dedicated mechanism be put in place to take care of
procedural or operational hurdles, if any, and resolve them expeditiously at the highest level of the
Ministry. The Committee wishes to be kept apprised of the progress of civil work on a quarterly
basis. (para 73)
All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), New Delhi
The Committee expresses its unhappiness at the tardy progress of implementation of the
project resulting in cost escalation as well as in surrendering of the budgeted funds. Keeping in view
the inordinate delay in operationalisation of this project, the Committee feels that the existing
system of monitoring leaves much to be desired and warrants a comprehensive review. Setting up of
the AIIA is a very ambitious project and is mandated to focus on very critical areas like fundamental
research, drug development, quality control etc. in Ayurveda. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that periodic/quarterly meetings should be held to review and constantly monitor the progress of
operationalisation of the Institute and resolve forthwith whatever procedural or administrative
hurdles are encountered in executing the project. The Committee also recommends the Ministry to
ensure that there is no further escalation of the project cost and the Institute should be fully
operationlised within the extended time frame. (para 76)
Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Development and Upgradation of AYUSH Institutions/
Colleges
Provision of Scheme
The Committee wonders why states governments are not able to avail the funds under this scheme.
The Committee notes that the scheme- Development and Upgradation of AYUSH Institutions has
been plagued with financial underperformance for the last many years, mainly due to pending UCs
and non-receipt of suitable proposals. In view of the fact that the Scheme has been restructured
and treasury route of funds has been adopted for transfer of funds, the Committee hopes that it
would lead to better financial performance. The Committee would, however, recommend that the
Ministry should ensure that the extent of grants made, actually results in corresponding development
and upgradation of AYUSH Institutions/Colleges. The Committee would like the Ministry to put in
place an effective monitoring mechanism for the purpose. (para 83)

Scheme for Grant-in-Aid to Non Profit/Non-Governmental AYUSH organizations/Institutions for
upgradation to Centres of Excellence
The Committee observes that this is yet another example of unrealistic projection of fund
requirements, which were left unutilized. The Committee notes with dismay that explaining the
reasons for variation between the budgetary provisions of Rs. 20.00 crore in BE and RE 2014-15
respectively and the savings to the extent of 15.83 crore the Ministry has stated that the "balance
upto RE level will be utilized in March, 2015" and not enumerated the specific reasons for huge

Research and Development including Medicinal Plants
The Committee observes that no amount of pure research will be useful unless it leads to
health outcomes and health products accruing therefrom, percolating to the ultimate beneficiaries
i.e the patients through health care delivery systems. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Ministry should evaluate all the on-going research projects on the basis of the above yardsticks
and apprise the Committee of the outcome thereof. (para 91)
National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB)
The Committee feels constrained to note that a substantial amount of funds are involved in
pending UCs under National Medicinal Plants Board (Central Sector Scheme) and National Mission
on Medicinal Plants (Centrally Sponsored Scheme). Of more serious concern is the fact the UCs
continue to be pending even under the Central Sector Scheme which is under the direct administrative
control of the Ministry. As regards the pendency of UCs under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme, the

have been able to develop an effective system of co-ordination with the State Governments for the

Quality Control of ASU&H Drugs
The Committee in its 55th Report on Demands for Grants (2012-13) of erstwhile Department
of AYUSH had inter-alia observed that "the quality and standardization of ASU&H products and
stringent implementation of the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and the rules
framed thereunder are very vital for the credibility of ASU&H drugs. However, the drug testing
requirements of ASU&H drugs cannot be met without setting up adequate number of quality control
laboratories and strengthening of the enforcement mechanisms of the States." From information
made available to the Committee, it is revealed that the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for supporting
quality control activities has been evaluated by an external agency and revised suitably on the basis
of suggestions from the States. The Committee sincerely hopes that the revised scheme would
maximize outcome oriented implementation and lead to better off-take under this scheme during

38
the remaining period of the 12th Five Year Plan. The Committee recommends that the Ministry
should closely monitor utilization of the funds under this head particularly, as it relates to capacity
building of the State Drug Testing Laboratories for better quality control of ASU&H drugs.
The Committee also notes that Indian Ayurvedic drugs were found containing excessive mercury
and other substance and therefore were banned by Eurpoean Union and some other Countries and
these Countries had imposed ban on Ayurvedic drugs and cosmetics which apart from bringing a bad
name to the country also resulted in loss of precious foreign exchange. The Committee recommends
that such incidents need to be avoided. (para 105)
The Committee observes that quality control and standardization of ASU&H drugs leaves
much to be desired. It has often been reported in the media that Ayurveda and Homoeopathy drugs,
which were given to patients for various ailments, were laced with steroids and other improper
drugs. Permissible limits of heavy metals, pesticide residue, microbial load etc. are also sometimes
breached and regulatory needs of standardization and quality control of ASU&H drugs get seriously
impaired. On the issue of setting up of a separate Drug Controller of AYUSH, the decision to
develop a vertical structure of AYUSH in the present Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation
(CDSCO) headed by the Drug Controller General of India is not acceptable to the Committee. The
Committee feels that in order to strengthen regulatory mechanism and effectively oversee the
quality control of ASU&H drugs, setting up of a separate Central Drug Controller for ASU&H drugs
is an imminent necessity since a wing of AYUSH in the existing CDSCO may not produce the
desired result of effective regulation of ASU&H drugs. The Committee is of the view that a separate
Central Drugs Controller of AYUSH will help synergise the core competencies of the Central and
State Regulatory Authorities by developing dynamic relation between them and also go a long way
in building credibility in ASU&H drugs besides promoting AYUSH in foreign countries. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that action be initiated to setup an independent and separate Central Drug
Controller for ASU&H drugs at the earliest. (para 108)
The Committee in its 55th Report on Demands for Grants 2012-13, had commented upon the
ineffectiveness of the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954. The
Report was presented on 26th April, 2012 and despite the Committee's repeated reference to this
issue, no substantive action had been taken till date. This is indicative of the Ministry's lackadaisical
approach towards this important issue. The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry has
finally constituted a Task Force for the purpose of suggesting amendments in the aforesaid Act. The
Committee would like the Ministry to play a proactive role in expediting the Report of the Task
Force so that the shortcomings witnessed in the aforesaid Act are addressed effectively. The
Committee also desires that early action may be taken to amend the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules,
1945. (para 114)
The Committee also observes that the Ministry should not be complacent by merely forwarding
the list of recalcitrant advertisers to the State Licensing authorities and instead acquaint itself with
the follow-up action taken by them. (para 115)

The Committee welcomes the restructuring of the Scheme - Information, Education and

Regulation of the education of Ayurveda, Siddha  and Unani (ASU) Systems of Medicine and

5. The Committee then heard the Secretary, Ministry of AYUSH on the Demands for Grants (2015-16)
of the Ministry. The Secretary made a power points presentation on the Demands of Grants (2015-16)
inter-alia highlighting the following points viz. the expenditure details from 2012-13 to 2014-15; measures
taken for optimal utilisation of budget 2014-15; steps taken for liquidation of utilisation Certificates with
States; percentage of utilisation of funds on NE, STs, SCs (2013-14; 2014-15); details of non plan expenditure
in the 12th Plan; important activities/milestones during the year 2014-15; quality control of Ayurveda, Siddha,
Unani and Homeopathy Drugs; International Co-operation in the field of Medicinal Plants; NMPB Activities
(2014-15); works relating to Medicinal Plants; achievements (2014-2015) and targets (2015-16) in Central
Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences, Central Council for Research in Homoeopathy, and Central
Council for Research in Unani Medicine, etc. Thereafter, Members raised a number of issues like road map
for growing medicinal plants; reasons for non existence of more private colleges in Ayurveda; reasons for
AYUSH not being made a popular area of practice; action being taken on misleading advertisements claiming
treatments for treating fatal diseases by use AUS&H medicines; reasons for classical AUS&H drugs not
being clinically tested; mechanism for interface between allopathic stream and National Medicinal Plants
Board.

Research; need to promote AUS&H in foreign countries, etc.

Welfare, having been authorized by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Eighty-
fifth Report of the Committee on the Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Acquired Immune Deficiency
Syndrome (Prevention And Control) Bill, 2014*.

States relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha,
referred** the Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (Prevention
and Control) Bill, 2014 ( Annexure-I) to the Committee on the 24th February, 2014, as introduced in the
Rajya Sabha on the 11th February, 2014 for examination and report within two months. However, the
previous Committee could not consider the Bill and present its Report due to dissolution of the 15th Lok
Sabha. Subsequently Hon'ble Chairman granted extension upto 30th April, 2015 for presentation of
Report on the Bill.

September, 18th September, 25th September, 27th November, 2014, 9th February, 10th February, 3rd

REPORT
1. The Human Immunodeficiency Virus and Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome hereinafter
referred to as the Bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 11th February 2014 and referred to the
Department- related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare on 24th February,
2014 for examination and report.
2. As per the information provided by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the first HIV/AIDS
Bill was drafted in 1989 and subsequently withdrawn as it contained provisions such as mandatory
testing and confinement of infected persons. Subsequently, in 2003, at an international conference
organized by NACO, the NGO Lawyers Collective was asked to develop a draft legislation on HIV. The
draft was completed by Lawyers Collective in 2006 and forwarded to NACO for further processing.
3. Since 2007, the Bill has been modified based on the inputs of the Legislative Department and also
from NACO. In addition, draft was also examined by the then-Solicitor General of India in 2010. By
2011, the HIV scenario in India had changed - the prevalence had reduced, the programme was scaled
up and service uptake was encouraging. Thus the draft was again modified by NACO and made more
concise. In 2012, comments on the Bill were sought from all departments of the Government of India
and the draft was subsequently modified again. The current Bill has been drafted to safeguard the rights
of the people living with HIV and affected by HIV. The Bill aims to enhance access to health care services
by ensuring informed consent and confidentiality for HIV-related testing, treatment and clinical research.
Furthermore, it was strongly felt that systems for redressing grievances need to be established. These
were long-term goals to ensure that an effective prevention, care, support and treatment programme was
implemented in the country.
4. Due to the change of Government in the year 2014, the matter was reconsidered by NACO and
the provisions were looked into. After approval of the then Minister of Health and Family Welfare, the
Note for Cabinet was sent to the Cabinet Secretariat for placing before the Cabinet. The Cabinet
Secretariat advised to obtain fresh Inter-Ministerial consultations. Thus, the Cabinet note was circulated
to all the Ministries/Departments with a copy to PMO for their comments. The issues that were raised
in the comments have been adequately dealt with and no changes have been made in the Cabinet Note.
The Ministry in its background note has mentioned the following as the salient highlights of Bill –
(i) Many instances of discrimination have been seen because a person is HIV- infected or
affected. The Bill aims to ensure that HIV status does not influence the right to education,
employment, health care and insurance. For example, the Bill seeks to prohibit HIV-testing
as a pre-requisite for employment, healthcare access or education.
(ii) Internationally, a rights-based approach (involving informed consent and voluntary disclosure
of HIV-status) is known to be effective in increasing access to services. The provisions in
the Bill ensure that HIV tests, treatment or research can only be conducted with the person's
informed consent.
(iii) Disclosure of one's HIV-status is a sensitive issue due to the stigma associated with sexual
transmission. The Bill aims to ensure that no one is compelled to disclose his/her status.
(iv) Many cases of discrimination have been observed in health-care settings which stem from
providers fearing infection as HIV positive people are under their care. The Bill provides for
training, Universal Precautions and Post Exposure Prophylaxis which can reduce instances
of discrimination in health care settings by addressing the fears of health care workers.

2
(v) Preventive efforts with Most at Risk Populations such as Sex Workers, Men-who-have-sex-
with-men, Transgender and Injecting Drug Users are at times disrupted because of law
enforcement. Provisions in the Bill ensure that efforts of NGOs working on HIV prevention
are not hampered and that necessary outreach is not interrupted.
(vi) National AIDS Control Organisation under the National AIDS Control Programme implements
a strong Antiretroviral Therapy (ART) programme, however its sustainability needs to be
ensured. The Bill has provisions which make a legal commitment on behalf of the Central
and State Governments to provide ART and management of related infections, as far as
possible.
(vii) As there is no platform for grievances and complaints related to HIV-status and health care,
the Bill provides for ombudspersons at the State level and Complaints Officers at the
institutional level to redress grievances related to provisions of Bill.
(viii) Schemes pertaining to people living with HIV need ownership of the State Governments and
different ministries and departments. The Bill puts an obligation on Central and State
governments to take measures to facilitate better access to welfare schemes for HIV-
affected persons.
(ix) Women living with and affected by HIV are often subject to discriminatory practices. The
Bill provides that they have the right to reside in the shared household, and receive counseling
regarding pregnancy so that they can make their own informed decisions.
(x) The Bill has sections aimed at benefiting children who are affected /orphaned by HIV and
AIDS. The Bill contains provisions to safeguard the property of HIV-affected children and
recognizes the guardianship of older siblings for admission to educational institutions, managing
property, operating bank accounts etc.
(xi) Court matters pertaining to PLHIV need to be dealt with sensitively. The bill aims to ensure
that HIV-positive persons, if convicted, shall be placed in custodial facilities where treatment
is available.
(xii) The Bill provides for the redressing of grievances and addressing contravention of the Bill's
provisions through the following mechanisms – i) One or more Ombudspersons appointed
by the State Governments; ii) Complaints Officers designated in establishments, including
healthcare institutions; (the manner in which Complaints Officers will deal with complaints
of violations under the Act will be prescribed in the Rules), iii) The court of a Judicial
Magistrate of First Class and through, iv) Systems established under legislations such as
Juvenile Justice Act, for example, the Child Welfare Committee (CWC).
(xiii) The Bill provides for a penalty for hatred and discriminatory propaganda against people
infected and affected by HIV . The penalty is imprisonment (which shall not be less than
three months but which may extend to two years) and a fine that may extend to One Lakh
rupees or both. In addition there are penalties (in the form of fines) for non-compliance of
orders of Ombudsman and also for breaching confidentiality in legal proceedings.
5. According to Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill, India is estimated to have 2.39 million
people living with HIV/AIDS (PLHIV), the third highest number after South Africa and Nigeria and the

3
epidemic is more prevalent in high-risk groups such as female sex workers, men-who-have-sex-with-
men and injecting drug users. It is, therefore, important for these groups to access services such as
treatment of sexually transmitted infections, HIV testing, condoms, clean needles and syringes to prevent
transmission of HIV to general population.
6. As the route of transmission is primarily sexual, there is a stigma arising out of HIV infection and
those affected by it, leading to discrimination which includes denial of, and access to, healthcare and
treatment; discrimination against admission or continuance of their children in schools; denial of, and/
or removal from, employment and denial of various services including insurances, medical benefits, etc.,
in both public and private establishments.
7. In view of the situation it was necessary to address the issue of stigma faced by those infected
by HIV and AIDS, to ensure confidentiality and privacy while providing HIV and AIDS related services
and to strengthen the existing National AIDS Control Programme by bringing in legal accountability. It
was also important that existing establishments, both private and public, recognize the need to safeguard
the rights of people infected with HIV/AIDS, particularly, women and children.
8. During the course of his oral evidence before the Committee on 9th February, 2015, Shri N.S.
Kang, Additional Secretary and DG, CGHS delineated the following points with reference to the Bill,
namely, (i) chronology of HIV/AIDS Bill; (ii) objectives of the Bill i.e. to remove stigma and discrimination
related to HIV/AIDS in the public and private sector, (iii) create an enabling environment for service
access; (iv) establish systems of grievance redressal by way of appointment of Ombudsman and complaints
officers; (v) key beneficiaries of the Bill, (vi) salient features of the Bill i.e. reducing HIV- related
discrimination; (vii) a rights -based approach involving informed consent and disclosure of HIV- status;
(viii) ensuring safety of Health Care Providers; (ix) reducing risk among Most at Risk Populations; (x)
legal commitment for treatment of HIV; (xi) promotion of Information, Education, Communication (IEC)
on HIV; (xii) penalties for HIV related hatred and discrimination; (xiii) welfare measures by the Government
including welfare of HIV-affected women and HIV- affected children, etc.
9. The Committee also heard the views of some stakeholders/experts on the provisions of the Bill.
The Committee received several memoranda from the stake holders on the provisions of the Bill. Some
of the views/amendments put forth by the Experts/Stakeholders before the Committee are listed below:
 To include most at risk population who have been left out in the definition of discrimination
in Section 2(d).
 To amend the definition of the term 'protected person' in Section 2(s) by addition of sub-
section (iv) which reads as follows " A sex worker, an injecting drug User, a man who has
sex with another man and a transgender person" or "most at Risk of HIV";
 To delete the word 'minor' from the definition of 'reasonable accommodation' in Section
2(t);
 Deletion of the words "as far as possible" from section 14 as the words are not inclusive
and goes against the rights based approach of treatment for all.
 Addition of the term "diagnostics" after "Anti-retroviral" in Clause 14.
 To replace the words "HIV status" with the terms "HIV related information" in Sections
8(l)(i), 8(1)

4
 Fixing a time frame of 15 days and in emergency, 24 hours for passing orders by the Health
Ombudsman with regard to the complaint made;
 Lowering the age of consent for HIV test and treatment from 18 to 16;
 Need for removal of offensive words like 'needles', people living with HIV in the provisions
pertaining to non-discrimination;
 Lack of clarity on the structure and linkages of Ombudsman and how binding would be
action taken by her/him'
 Co-infections should be mentioned in the present Bill;
 Emphasis must be placed on protection of data collected and analysed for prevention and
spread of disease; etc.
Presentation by the Forum of Pariiamentarians on HIV/AIDS
10. During the course of his oral evidence before the Committee on the 19th March, 2015, Shri Oscar
Fernandes, MP and President, Forum of Parliamentarians on HIV/AIDS in India (FPA) gave a brief
account on the role of the Forum. Thereafter, Shri J.D. Seelam, MP, a member of the Forum  highlighted
the following points on the Bill, namely,  (a) need to include a new sub-section (iv) in Clause 2(S)
(Protected Person) which may be framed as "Most vulnerable to HIV"; (b) need to include Sub-section
(iv) in Clause  2(D) (Discrimination)  which may be framed  as "Most vulnerable to HIV"; (c) need to
partially shift the burden of proving discrimination to the person alleged to have discriminated by inserting
the following provisions in the Bill "When the question is whether a person has been discriminated under
this Act and it is shown that the person against whom such discrimination is alleged to have taken place
is a protected person and that the act or omission alleged as being discriminatory took place, the Court
shall presume, unless the contrary is proved, that such act or omission is discrimination under this Act.";
(d) need to replace the term "possible" with "feasible" and addition of term diagnostic after "antiretroviral"
in clause 14; (e) need to reduce the age of consent to 16 years for HIV test and treatment in Clause
22; (f) need to make provision for procedure for receiving evidence or procedure for enforcement in
Clause 23-24  (Health Ombudsman); (g) need to make certain additions to the Grievance Redressal
Mechanism by Complaints Officer in Clause 21 on the following lines viz. disposal of complaints in time-
bound manner, empowering complaints Officer to issue order for sensitization and counselling of accused
persons under the HIV , taking suo-motu cognizance of breach of HIV/AIDS law at an institutional level;
and (h) need to make the Bill gender neutral, etc.
11. The various suggestions/views/amendments put forth before the Committee were forwarded to the
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare for its comments. A statement containing the suggestions/views/
amendments proposed by various stake holders and response of the Ministry thereto is placed at
Annexure-I.

of the Members of the Committee. The Committee's observations and recommendations contained in the
Report reflect an extensive scrutiny of all the viewpoints put forth before it. Upon examination of the
comments received from the Ministry, the Committee makes the following suggestions/ recommendations:-

2(c) "child affected by HIV" means a person below the age of eighteen years, who is HIV-positive

children orphaned by AIDS.

"2 (g) "guidelines" means any statement or any other document issued by the Central Government

CHAPTER II - Prohibition of Certain Acts
17. Clause 3
3 (j) the denial of, or unfair treatment in, the provision of insurance unless such unfair treatment

Suggestions
18. The Committee has received suggestions for inclusion of a provision in Clause 3 that no person
affected with HIV/AIDS will be denied both life as well as health insurance on the count of merely his/
her being HIV/AIDS positive and such person shall have the right to life as well as medical insurance.
Any claim by such persons shall not be denied.

19. The Ministry has informed that such a provision already exists in the Bill in Clause 3(j).They have

insurance to all the HIV positive people. However, the IRDA was not in favour of providing insurance
cover to such persons at normal rate of premium.
Observation/Recommendation
20. The Committee is of the opinion that all HIV positive people should be provided insurance
cover without any discrimination preferably at normal rate of premium or they may be charged
slightly higher rate of premium but in no case exorbitant rate of premium should be charged

6
from HIV positive people for providing insurance cover for both life and health insurance. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should pursue the matter with the IRDA

words 'such unfair treatment is based on and' may be deleted in order to make the provision
